title: SeededGrasp: Language-Guided Grasping in Complex Scenes with Multiple Embodiments
hook: Instead of one giant end-to-end model, let the VLM just point — predict a seed point, then hand off to a lightweight grasp generator. Data-efficient, and it transfers across robot hands.
key_points: Splits grasping in two: a VLM does high-level semantic reasoning and predicts a seed point; a lightweight model turns that seed into a grasp.
Decoupling avoids expensive end-to-end VLM-plus-grasp training, so it's far more data-efficient than joint approaches.
The seed-point conditioning lets one system support multiple embodiments — different grippers — in cluttered scenes.
Ships what the authors call the first multi-embodiment tabletop grasping dataset: over 2.5M grasps in cluttered scenes.
Reports 72% grasp success in simulation and 78% in real-world experiments, beating prior baselines.
content_html: Robotic grasping in cluttered scenes needs both 3D spatial reasoning and an understanding of what the task actually asks for. SeededGrasp, from a University of Toronto group, gets there without one monolithic model: a vision-language model reads the scene and the instruction and predicts a single seed point, which then conditions a lightweight grasp-generation model. Splitting high-level semantic reasoning from low-level geometric execution keeps training cheap and lets the same system drive different robot hands.
extra_html:
How it works

Existing language-guided grasping either asks a VLM to predict the grasp directly — with limited spatial awareness — or trains the VLM and grasp model jointly, which is data- and compute-hungry. SeededGrasp instead uses the VLM only to pick a seed point from the scene and instruction; a small downstream model turns that point into a full grasp for whatever gripper is in use. To train it, the authors release what they describe as the first multi-embodiment tabletop grasping dataset, over 2.5 million grasps in cluttered scenes.

Why it matters

The decoupling is the transferable idea: let a big pretrained model handle semantics and let a specialized, cheap model handle geometry. The authors report 72% grasp success in simulation and 78% in real-world experiments, ahead of prior baselines, while supporting multiple embodiments — a combination end-to-end approaches had struggled to scale. Code and data are on the project site.

related.title: Geometric Action Model: One Backbone for Geometry and Action
related.hook: GAM turns a pretrained 3D-geometry model into a robot's brain - a single backbone that forecasts both future geometry and the actions to get there, beating heavier VLA baselines.

related.title: π0: A Vision-Language-Action Model
related.hook: π0 is a generalist robot policy: it takes camera images, joint angles, and a plain-language instruction, and outputs smooth action sequences — folding laundry, bussing tables, bagging groceries.

flashcards.prompt: How does SeededGrasp split the grasping problem into two stages?
flashcards.back_html: A vision-language model does the high-level semantic reasoning and predicts a seed point; a separate lightweight model turns that seed into the actual grasp.

flashcards.prompt: Why is SeededGrasp more data-efficient than training the VLM and grasp model together?

choices.text: It decouples semantic reasoning from grasp generation, avoiding costly end-to-end training
It uses a smaller VLM with far fewer parameters
It drops the vision-language model entirely at inference time

flashcards.explanation_html: The VLM only predicts a seed point that conditions a lightweight grasp model, sidestepping the data and compute of joint end-to-end training.

flashcards.prompt: What does SeededGrasp's seed-point design enable beyond a single robot?
flashcards.back_html: Support for multiple embodiments — different grippers — since the lightweight downstream model handles per-embodiment geometry while the VLM's seed point stays high-level.
